title: Does a learned model beat the dumbest available rule at predicting when a GPS broadcast ephemeris will be badly wrong?

scope.one_line: GPS only. ESA final orbit and clock products. A contiguous run of days, split TEMPORALLY - earlier days train, strictly later days test. One seed. One threshold definition.
scope.corpus: Broadcast navigation from BKG (BRDC00IGS mixed-constellation RINEX 3), precise orbits from ESA0OPSFIN ORB.SP3 and precise clocks from ESA0OPSFIN 30S CLK.CLK. All public, no auth.
scope.seed: Single seed recorded in the artifact. Not a variance study.
scope.unit: One (satellite, epoch) pair: a broadcast record evaluated at a future epoch.
scope.receiver_emulation: The ephemeris used at epoch t is the most recent one whose transmission time precedes t - what a real receiver actually holds - NOT the record with the closest toe. Pipeline validation used closest-toe, which pinned age-of-data near zero and made its effect unobservable; that reading was recorded as COULD NOT VERIFY and this preregistration fixes it.
scope.what_this_does_not_cover: It does not cover other constellations, other analysis centres, or real-time/rapid products. It does not test the scaling curve, G4 under the effort lens, or the buyer. Passing A2 clears ONE gate and makes no claim about viability. It also does not establish that the SISRE convention used here - standard global-average weights, per-satellite median clock bias removed as unobservable to a receiver - matches any particular service's definition.

auc_margin.passes_if: learned_auc - best_baseline_auc >= 0.05, where best_baseline_auc is the maximum over the FROZEN baseline set

arms: THE FROZEN BASELINE SET, built and measured before any learned number is believed. Adding a stronger baseline afterwards is allowed and must be reported SEPARATELY; it may not replace this set, and it may not be dropped if it wins.
NULL CONTROL: labels shuffled, identical pipeline retrained, must fall to AUC <= 0.55.

TEMPORAL SPLIT as the rival explanation run as an arm. A random split over epochs lets the model see the same satellite on the same day and measures memorisation of a slowly varying state rather than prediction. This is the direct analogue of the grouped-split clause that caught a 0.4873 to 0.1531 collapse in the archived trial.
AGE-OF-DATA, made observable by receiver emulation. Physics says broadcast error must grow with it; if the corrected pipeline still shows nothing, that is a finding about the label.
stop_rules: If the learned model does not beat the best frozen baseline by 0.05 AUC, A2 FAILS and EphemErr joins the other five candidates that died at this gate. That is published as a failure.
If the null control exceeds AUC 0.55 the pipeline is discarded and no number from it is reported.
If the split is not temporal the gate fails however good the numbers are.
Passing A2 clears ONE gate and licenses no claim about viability.
why_a2_is_the_whole_question: Five candidates across rounds 1-3 died because a rule anyone could write by hand already owned the label, and none of them expected it: a 50-line COBOL rule at F1 0.768, a nearest-centroid ISA classifier at 93.9% with no training loop, an eight-line census rule at AUC 0.83 with zero training records, and a 15-line regex beating the 'honest' genome baseline by 30 points. Round 2 recorded EphemErr's A2 as ENTIRELY UNMEASURED and named URA/SISA as the likely killer. Pipeline validation has since measured URA's rank correlation with SISRE at -0.077 - essentially nothing - and found a different dominant baseline round 2 never named: SATELLITE IDENTITY, which separates G28 at 0.300 m residual std from G21 at 12.592 m. Both are in the frozen baseline set.
frozen_baseline_set: PER-SATELLITE historical mean |SISRE|, computed on train days only. Identified during pipeline validation as the true dominant baseline, and the one round 2 missed.
URA/SISA broadcast index alone - the operator's own error bound, shipped free in the student input
per-satellite historical mean combined with age-of-data
